video_title: The Birth & Rise of India's IT Outsourcing Industry
transcript: It is perhaps one of history's most  unlikely industrial success stories. India was desperately poor - a  largely agricultural nation with   weak infrastructure running a heavily  regulated socialist economic model. Yet somehow, a number of billion dollar  Indian tech giants managed to emerge.   And through them, India became a  monster IT service export powerhouse. Offshoring continues to  strike strong emotions today.   In today’s video, we look at the rise  of the Indian IT export industry. ## Coauthors Before we start, I want to thank my  coauthor, Zoso/Felix of the Zoso Project. I have been following his X feed for some time  now and am impressed by his unique perspective.   I don't always agree but I  have to think about it first. Go check out his work, which includes the  companion pieces to this video - headed by   this provocative image. Alright on with the show. ## Beginnings By the 1960s, India's Tata Group  had grown into a massive industrial   giant with firms like the Tata Iron  and Steel Company and Tata Motors. These companies had significant data processing  needs. Seeing how the West increasingly valued   such data processing work, Chairman JRD Tata's  brother-in-law, aide, and friend Colonel Leslie   Sawhney proposed an in-house unit to process  data for all the Tata Group’s companies. JRD approved and the new,  then unnamed firm was seeded   with staff from Tata Administrative  Service. They hired several talented,   quantitatively minded folks from  MIT and other top universities. In 1966, they moved into one of India's  first skyscrapers - the Nirmal Building in   south Bombay - and set up two IBM 1401s and an  ICL 1903. Thus began the Tata Computer Center. But soon afterwards, Sawhney passed -  leaving the new firm rudder-less and   without its key champion within  the larger Tata conglomerate. The Tata firms listened to presentations  but remained weary of the new unit and   passed relatively little work, mostly  relating to shareholder services.   The only exception being Tata  Electric - the group's power utility.   With costs rising, the unit  began taking on external clients. Their consulting work spanned the gamut. For  instance, they advised the Tata Institute of   Social Sciences on how to structure,  administer and analyze surveys - but   whatever they were doing they were good  enough to win customers away from IBM. In 1968, Tata Sons - the group's core holding  company - restructured their consulting and   service firms into four operating units. One of  these units was Tata Consultancy Services or TCS.   Afterwards, TCS received two top managers  from Tata Electric - Director PM Agarwala   and General Manager Faqir Chand (F.C.) Kohli. ## Tata Consultancy Services TCS began as a young rowdy company with lots of   potential but perhaps not the most  discipline, especially with cash. In light of that, Kohli - a brilliant  technocrat who cut his teeth running the   city's power grid - was the right person to  bring on. He initially did not want to come   run TCS - he eyed the head job at Tata  Electric - but was eventually coerced. Kohli studied the firm for six  months, then made a fateful change.   As customer companies were not  initially interested in data processing,   TCS first pitched them management consulting  services and upsold the data processing later. In 1973, Indira Gandhi's government - then  suffering a fiscal deficit - passed the   Foreign Exchange Regulation Act. FERA imposed  strict regulations on imports and exports.   Moreover, it famously restricted  foreign ownership in JVs to only 40%. One of the companies affected was the American  firm Burroughs. The firm's managers wanted to   enter India, but needed a partner. After building  a strong personal relationship with Kohli,   they chose to partner with Tata Sons for a  JV producing Burroughs software and hardware. So in 1974, TCS imported one of Burroughs'  computers, a B1728 costing $300,000.   The government's Software Export Scheme  allowed companies to import such hardware,   but it also committed them to  earning back double the import price   in software export revenues  over the next five years. TCS intended to earn that back developing  software for Burroughs - including   migrating older software  to new hardware platforms. Porting was a major initial category for  the Indian IT outsourcers. Drab and tedious,   yet also requiring paying close  attention to every line in the code.   It contributed some 20-40%  of their early business. One of their first overseas engagements  was a $24,000 project porting a hospital   accounting package written in Burroughs medium  systems COBOL to Burroughs small systems COBOL. This project and others were delivered using a  combination of development work done in India   and onsite efforts done by TCS workers flown  right to the United States. This latter practice   would become widespread in the Indian IT export  industry and is today known as "body shopping". ## Setting Up In the United States As I briefly mentioned earlier,   Tata struck a joint venture with Burroughs  to import and make their hardware. In 1977, the Indian government finally granted  Tata the license to manufacture Burroughs   computers. But after all that work, the Tata Sons  office decided against manufacturing computers. Instead, they set up a separate JV company  called Tata Burroughs that would import and   sell Burroughs computers into India. To some,  this was a missed opportunity for an Indian   company to actually start making computer  hardware. They kind of took the easy way out. Anyway. Tata Burroughs' sudden  appearance threatened TCS' existence.   Why have two separate software and  consulting houses operating inside Tata? But FC Kohli pushed back hard, and it was  eventually agreed that TCS can retain its   independence. However it had to find its own  book of business outside of the Burroughs work.   With this, a challenge became an opportunity. In the late 1970s, TCS set up its first  New York office and sent over Subramanian   Ramadorai - a rising star in the organization -  to be the sales manager. Armed with little but   a thin portfolio of Burroughs work, Ramadorai  diligently typed letters and sought business. The first big contract he landed was with the  Institutional Group Information Corporation,   an American financial data  processing consortium owned by banks.   Indian engineers can work while New York  slept - enabling a 24-hour dev cycle.   IGIC became a willing reference for  future customers like American Express. By 1980, Tata Consultancy and Tata Burroughs had  emerged as India's two top software exporters -   accounting for over 60% of the $4 million  of exports. 19 or so firms shared the rest. ## IBM's Departure Since 1951 when it founded a marketing  and support office in Calcutta,   IBM had been India’s dominant computer company. In the 1960s, the company rented  digital computers like its IBM 1401   using its usual full-service rental  model encompassing hardware, software,   and maintenance. They lapped the  field in terms of computer counts. But the government grew dissatisfied -  feeling that IBM treated their country   as a "dumping ground" for old, outdated machines.  The company negotiated with the Department of   Electronics on items like tech transfer, but  eventually came to a non-negotiable matter. That matter was IBM owning 100%  share of its Indian subsidiary.   Per the aforementioned FERA law, that share  must be diluted down to 40%. Britain's ICL,   the other large foreign computer company,  complied but IBM stood their ground. It had less to do with control - IBM  can still exercise full control with   only 40% - than the fact that  it was their global policy.   In 1977, things came to a head, and IBM  finally announced that it will leave. Other companies like the boomer  drink Coca-Cola did the same. Customers who already had IBM machines were  allowed to keep them after paying 3 months' rent.   Spares and inventory were sold off to a  newly formed maintenance company called CMC.   And IBM India employees got six months  of salary plus more as a goodbye. IBM's departure abruptly created a void  that many tried to fill. In hindsight,   many of the actual opportunities that emerged  had little to do with what IBM once did.   But the perception that such  opportunities existed was enough. ## Patni and Patni Computer Systems Narendra Patni was a clean-cut man  with a big smile and relaxed look. The son of a grain merchant,   he did his undergraduate studies at India's  elite University of Roorkee. Then in 1964,   he received a scholarship to go to the  United States for a masters at MIT. Whilst working at Forrester Consulting  Group, a marketing and research firm,   Patni got interested in academic publishing.  He noticed how manual the process of encoding   manuscripts to digital data, and thought  that it could be done in India for less. After a trial run with India and America  represented by separate bedrooms,   Patni and his wife founded an  outsourcing business for data conversion. Then in the 1970s, IBM’s troubles in India  plus changing business conditions spurred a   shift to smaller minicomputers. DEC, Wang Labs  and others itched to enter the Indian market. Through his Boston connections, Patni struck  a partnership with Data General - an early   minicomputer firm. So in 1976, he and his  two brothers founded a new company called   Patni Computer Systems or PCS  to import these minicomputers. Per Indian policy, PCS had to "earn back"  this hardware with software exports,   so they wrote or ported  application software for clients.   In 1979, PCS won a $500,000 deal  porting and developing new features   for a software application called comprehensive  apparel manufacturer’s package (CAMP). Made by a firm called Data Basics,   CAMP was a kind of proto-ERP that US companies  used to manage textile imports from Asia.   The engagement was successful and led  to additional work with Data Basics. ## Patni to Infosys The man leading the effort at  PCS was N. R. Narayana Murthy,   hired back in 1977 to be general manager  of PCS' growing software business. A talented programmer and devout Hindu,  Murthy had once before started his own company   selling software in India but failed.  At PCS, he handled three jobs at once:   Data center management, computer sales  in India, and software export sales. After four years of doing this and  visiting and understanding the US market,   he felt that he was ready to  try starting another company.   And believed that if he didn't do it  before turning 35, he would be cooked. Six of his colleagues ended up joining him.   Funded with $250 from Murthy's wife, they  started Infosys in July 1981. The new business   quickly won over PCS's best customer Data  Basics, which sold the CAMP software. But in those early days, Infosys did not have  enough money to buy their own computer to do   software development. So the company sent all  of its cofounders except Murthy to America   to work physically at the  client site. More body-shopping. ## Changing Times: A Focus on Software India's IT sector grew within a socialist-minded,   nationalist framework that  emphasized self-reliance. Nothing wrong with that, but there comes a  line when self-reliance tips into autarky.   By the mid-1980s, the Indian economy was  suffering from stifled growth and isolation.   Then came a series of major developments that  unlocked and supercharged the IT exports industry. First, we had government reform.   In 1984, Rajiv Gandhi was elected as Prime  Minister after his mother's assassination.   Gandhi was technically savvy - a booster of  technology - and experienced first-hand the   issues of India's electronics policies whilst  organizing the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi. His administration passed a series of new liberal  policies favoring software and hardware imports.   Tariffs on PCs imported for developing software  were cut from 135% to just 60%, and then zero a   few years later. Software tools for developing  other export software can be imported duty-free. Many of these liberalizations were somewhat  walked back due to unstable economic and political   situations. Taxes on software and foreign travel  were hiked back up, for instance. But what stuck   helped software exports reach $96 million in 1990  - up from just $3.5 million ten years earlier. Once upon a time, India's Department  of Electronics saw its role   as regulating electronics production and  protecting domestic manufacturing - i.e.   coddling India's biggest computer  manufacturer, ECIL. But in the 1980s,   that attitude shifted to promoting  software exports and private investment. ## Changing Times: Software Parks Second were the Software  Technology Parks, or STPs. The concept of an export processing  zone enjoying duty-free privileges   on imported equipment and relaxed labor  statutes isn't new even within India.   India was in fact one of the first Asian  countries to have them with the KASEZ in Gujarat. A particularly special one was the Santacruz  Electronics EPZ in Mumbai. Created back in   1973 for electronics manufacturing, a few  software companies made their way there. Citibank opened a software development  subsidiary inside. TCS and Tata Burroughs too.   The EDA firm Gateway Design Automation was there  too in be 1980s - they are perhaps most known   for producing the hardware  design language Verilog. Some government officials started thinking about  a special zone to encourage software exports.   They would have the same duty-free and  labor privileges, but most importantly   the zones would have better  communication links with the US. Few things more personified India's issues  than its massive communications problem.   The Indian telecommunications sector was  just not good. At the time it was perhaps   the world's most archaic, inadequate, overloaded  and inefficient phone system. The waiting list   for a landline telephone connection stretched half  a million long, and took 2-5 years of waiting. Without more robust communications,   the Indian IT exports industry had no  choice but to rely on body-shopping.   Up into the late 1980s, 75-80% of India's  export earnings still came from body-shopping. So it was a big deal when  Texas Instruments in 1985   installed a satellite data link between  the US and the Indian city of Bangalore.   They saw India as a good potential  market, a place for talent,   and they wanted to use the time zone differences  to achieve a 24-hour development cycle. To get this satellite link installed, the  Indian Department of Electronics went to   bat for Texas Instruments. Hard. One DOE  veteran proudly said that they "broke 26   separate rules to accommodate TI's Bangalore  subsidiary and are willing to break more". Like for instance, by law only the  Department of Telecommunications can   own and operate earth station equipment.  So the DOE worked out a paper agreement   where TI paid for the equipment but the  department ran and rented it out to TI. Recognizing that campuses with shared resources  for compute, data communications links,   and other infrastructure can be a massive  boon for the software export industry,   the DOE began promoting the  Software Technology Parks in 1986. However, the parks would not actually come  into being until 1991 - due to infighting   over the critical communications  links. But their data connections   helped the Indian IT giants leave behind  their old body-shopping practices. Body shopping held a poor reputation.   It was also made less feasible by rule  changes in the early 1990s regarding   the US B-1 business visitor visa plus concerns  about the companies’ best talents hopping off. Better communications enabled what Tata  Consultancy called the "offshore model".   A small team travels to the client site to collect  requirements and implement solutions. Meanwhile,   most of the development work is done in India,   where salaries are a third that  of what they are in the West. It is true that Tata has been practicing  something like this since the earliest days   of their export service engagements. But then,   code had to be passed back and forth in  pouches by human couriers on flights.   Satellite comms links in the Software Parks  unlocked the offshore model’s full potential. It also enabled new higher-value  services like business process   services outsourcing and call centers.  Onsite work - the long-disdained body   shopping - fell from 80+% in the late  1980s to just 59% by the late 1990s. ## Changing Times: Liberalizations The STP policy arrived just before the more  famous 1991 liberalization - which had been   triggered by a significant  balance of payments crisis. The liberalizations dismantled the  old License Raj, devalued the rupee,   and reduced barriers to foreign investment.  Foreign companies like Oracle, IBM, and HP   now had the opportunity to come to India to  setup their own software development shops. The liberalizations also allowed  companies like Infosys to raise capital.   Infosys for their part went public in 1993  and used the money to build out their campus. The flood of foreign hardware triggered by the  lowering of trade barriers also forced companies   like Wipro and Hindustan Computers Limited  to adopt the IT services export model. Famously, Wipro was a vegetable oils manufacturer   that entered into minicomputers  and PCs after IBM's exit. After 1991, they became an engineering  lab for hire - writing code for embedded   applications in telecom gear and computers   before moving to generalized software development  services for banks, retailers, and manufacturers. Similar story for HCL. Founded by several  engineers who left behind another hardware maker,   HCL first made calculators and PCs. After  the import wave hit, they reorganized their   business around porting, driver development, and  onsite work. The hardware was later spun-off. Together, Wipro and HCL or HCLTech - plus  a fifth named Tech Mahindra - round out   India's major IT services export giants.  Over 90% of their revenues come from abroad. ## I must always mention UNIX The third (or fourth, I guess) factor I want  to bring up here might seem a bit strange,   but I think it is somewhat  underrated. India adopted UNIX. UNIX is the famous operating system  created inside AT&T's Bell Labs.   It broke ground as a convenient programming  environment in which people can develop software,   but more importantly, its source code was widely  accessible in a sort of proto-open source way. This was perfect for 1970s India. Imports  of finished software were restricted,   but source code imports were not.  Minicomputer makers like DCM and HCL   rapidly adopted UNIX - particularly  the Berkeley UNIX variant. This allowed a generation of Indian programmers  to gain deep familiarity with UNIX - an effect   further enhanced by the Reserve Bank  of India famously recommending UNIX   as the standard OS for India's banks in 1985. This familiarity became a boon when a  litany of UNIX variants like Sun's Solaris,   IBM's AIX, and HP's HP-UX became widely  embedded in the US corporate IT space.   Indian firms can develop on whatever  UNIX hardware they had, knowing   that it can work at a customer  site if they are also using UNIX. ## Y2K The Y2K crisis was going to be the  end of the world. That time of urgency   with dogs eating cats, water flowing up into the  sky, and big pillars of light like in the movies. Okay, maybe not. But fateful decisions by COBOL  developers to use two digits for a year to save   a little memory turned into what appeared  to be a looming disaster for computing. Ah, so few things are more poetic  than a tiny, innocuous decision   coming around to bite us all in the butt. Efforts to fix the "millennium bug" were  estimated to cost billions of dollars.   Were there even enough computer programmers in the  US to do it? The shortage seemed so severe that   the US government even raised its H-1 quota from  65,000 in 1998 to 115,000 in 1999 to handle it. The Indian IT giants identified  Y2K as a massive opportunity.   They advertised in the US, emphasizing the  potential savings of using Indian labor.   Tata Consultancy set up a "Y2K office" in  Chennai dedicated solely to fixing Y2K code. Each day, a thousand programmers churned out 2  million lines of COBOL code via a semi-automated,   17-step process, fixing Y2K bugs line by line. All in all, Y2K made some $2.3 billion for the  Indian software industry in the late 1990s. TCS'   revenues soared from $125 million in 1995 to $419  million in 1999, whilst maintaining 32% margins.   Infosys earned over 20% of its 1998  and 1999 revenues just from Y2K. In 1999, Infosys became the first Indian  company to issue ADRs on the US stock markets.   It allowed them to pay US employees in stock and  built up credibility with potential clients. And   it was just a good time to go public. The IPO was a hit. The stock soared  nearly 50% from the offering price   and continued climbing soon after. By the end  of 1999, the stock had risen 10 times from   its IPO - giving the company a $20 billion market  cap and newfound prominence in the United States. The other major IT outsourcer, TCS,  would be taken public a few years   later in 2004 - raising $1.2 billion in what  was then the largest IPO in Indian history. ## Post-Y2K The impressive results from the Y2K drive  created many engineers trained in FORTRAN,   COBOL and other languages. This convinced many customers to sign long  term agreements - generating repeat business   to maintain their software applications.  By 2001, over a quarter of the Fortune   1000 offshored their work - saving  up to 55% on their costs doing so. Big companies like Hewlett-Packard,  Dell, Oracle, Microsoft, and Cisco   announced aggressive expansions  into India - investing billions   of dollars and creating tens of  thousands of new Indian jobs. General Electric was a particularly notable  early adopter. After India liberalized in 1991,   GE made substantial early investments  - using Indian labor to help design   new fridges or jet engines at  half the cost of American labor. Though they preferred to say  that they were getting 100%   more people onto a task. Potato, potahto. In the 1990s, GE by itself contributed  50% of Wipro's software revenue   and 20-30% of Infosys' - a critical  booster in Indian credibility. In mid-2005,   the WSJ reported that GE still accounted for 15%  of Tata Consultancy Services' overseas revenue. By 2001, India had 19 software parks. Fueled by  all this new money flooding into the country,   cities like Bangalore turned into boomtowns.   People started saying that India  had a Silicon Valley of its own. ## The Offshoring Debate All this offshoring led to debates whether  India was stealing jobs from Americans. Back in 2000, the companies explained their  offshoring as filling a talent gap - they said   it was "almost impossible" to find enough  good developers. Indian labor can fill the gap   by making software and services cheaper -  thus making American labor more productive. But then the macroeconomy suffered a downturn in  2001 after the dotcom and telecom bubbles popped.   Companies then offshored their back offices -  maybe hiring an IT vendor like Wipro or TCS,   or opening their own India-based offices. It was  not so easy to argue talent shortage anymore. By 2003, stories of job migration over  to India began hitting the mainstream.   Business Week broke the plane in February 2003  with a cover story titled "The New Global Job   Shift" - contrasting the boom in Bangalore  with that of decline in the United States. That article asked: Can America lose these  critical knowledge work-based jobs like basic   research, chip design, and financial analysis and  still remain a global power? It cited an analyst   from Forrester Group saying that 3.3 million jobs  and $136 billion in wages will shift offshore. The story got more attention throughout the year.  Tales of Americans training their replacements   before they lose their jobs went mainstream,  and it started to garner political attention. For instance. In November 2003,  US Senator John Kerry - later 2004   US Presidential candidate and ketchup  scion (by marriage) - forwarded a bill   that would require call center workers to  identify where they physically were located.   Bad press canceled a 2003 Indiana  state government contract with Tata. And the issue featured prominently  during the 2004 US presidential election,   with Kerry attacking incumbent President  Bush's stances on offshoring and pledging   to close "tax loopholes" that made it happen.  He called such companies "Benedict Arnolds". There is no doubt that the stories hit hard  emotionally. Imagine how they might do on   TikTok today! Yet at the same time, the  data struggles to confirm on the aggregate   that offshoring actually leads to  layoffs, or that it is beneficial. Numbers and methodologies  differ between researchers   too. Economists point out how impossible  it is to truly know whether those new   Indian workers actually replaced work  done or previously done by an American. They also mention the recent post-bubble  recessions, rises in US worker productivity,   and also the fact that as India's  IT exports industry grows, they buy   more services from the US too. I shall  leave the debate to the comment section. ## Conclusion In 2003, India delivered $9.5 billion of exports.   By 2013, that had grown to about $76  billion. And then in 2023, $194 billion. Today, the sector as a whole is  directly responsible for 6 million jobs,   and 7-8% of India's GDP. With much of  that revenue still coming from abroad,   IT services exports offset  60% of India's trade deficit. As late as 2023, the industry grew a fairly  strong 8.4%. But then in 2024 growth rapidly   decelerated to 3.8% - incremental revenue  falling from $19 billion to $9 billion. Headcount growth slowed too. In 2023, the industry  as a whole added almost 300,000 jobs, per Nasscom.   A year later in 2024, it added only 60,000. The biggest companies posted headcount declines.   In 2024, Infosys saw headcount reduced  by about 26,000 via attrition and reduced   hiring - the first such decline in the  company's record as a public entity. Tata Consultancy's headcount declined by 13,000  in 2024 - the first decline since 2005. Then in   July 2025, they laid off 2% or 12,000 of their  employees - the company's largest layoff to date. And of course, the stock. Since December 2024,  the share prices of both Infosys and TCS have   declined 40%. Their price multiples  compressing significantly as well. This has been primarily attributed to AI. I  am struck by how similar the early jobs done   by Claude are to those ones done by the  IT exporters: Porting software, 24-hour   development cycles by submitting a long-running  job before going to bed, and other knowledge work. The risk is that the LLMs eventually do  all the things that the IT exporters can.   Announcements from Anthropic of Claude plugins  for legal, finance and sales tasks in early 2026   not only sledgehammered the SaaS  stocks, but Infosys and TCS as well. For what it is worth, the IT giants  have said that Generative AI will   eventually enhance rather than replace their work.   Enterprise customers still need integration,  governance, and trust. Productivity   going up will create savings that can be passed  to the client and additional margins to be kept. But reaching that place will require  a crossover - and wading through that   fast-flowing river will be challenging. The  giants are now making their way through it,   and we shall see if they  all make it through intact.

Indian engineers can work while New York  slept - enabling a 24-hour dev cycle.
IGIC became a willing reference for  future customers like American Express.
By 1980, Tata Consultancy and Tata Burroughs had  emerged as India's two top software exporters -
accounting for over 60% of the $4 million  of exports. 19 or so firms shared the rest.
## IBM's Departure
Since 1951 when it founded a marketing  and support office in Calcutta,
IBM had been India’s dominant computer company.
In the 1960s, the company rented  digital computers like its IBM 1401
using its usual full-service rental  model encompassing hardware, software,
and maintenance. They lapped the  field in terms of computer counts.
But the government grew dissatisfied -  feeling that IBM treated their country
as a "dumping ground" for old, outdated machines.  The company negotiated with the Department of
Electronics on items like tech transfer, but  eventually came to a non-negotiable matter.
That matter was IBM owning 100%  share of its Indian subsidiary.
Per the aforementioned FERA law, that share  must be diluted down to 40%. Britain's ICL,
the other large foreign computer company,  complied but IBM stood their ground.
It had less to do with control - IBM  can still exercise full control with
only 40% - than the fact that  it was their global policy.
In 1977, things came to a head, and IBM  finally announced that it will leave.
Other companies like the boomer  drink Coca-Cola did the same.
Customers who already had IBM machines were  allowed to keep them after paying 3 months' rent.
Spares and inventory were sold off to a  newly formed maintenance company called CMC.
And IBM India employees got six months  of salary plus more as a goodbye.
IBM's departure abruptly created a void  that many tried to fill. In hindsight,
many of the actual opportunities that emerged  had little to do with what IBM once did.
But the perception that such  opportunities existed was enough.
## Patni and Patni Computer Systems
Narendra Patni was a clean-cut man  with a big smile and relaxed look.
The son of a grain merchant,
he did his undergraduate studies at India's  elite University of Roorkee. Then in 1964,
he received a scholarship to go to the  United States for a masters at MIT.
Whilst working at Forrester Consulting  Group, a marketing and research firm,
Patni got interested in academic publishing.  He noticed how manual the process of encoding
manuscripts to digital data, and thought  that it could be done in India for less.
After a trial run with India and America  represented by separate bedrooms,
Patni and his wife founded an  outsourcing business for data conversion.
Then in the 1970s, IBM’s troubles in India  plus changing business conditions spurred a
shift to smaller minicomputers. DEC, Wang Labs  and others itched to enter the Indian market.
Through his Boston connections, Patni struck  a partnership with Data General - an early
minicomputer firm. So in 1976, he and his  two brothers founded a new company called
Patni Computer Systems or PCS  to import these minicomputers.
Per Indian policy, PCS had to "earn back"  this hardware with software exports,
so they wrote or ported  application software for clients.
In 1979, PCS won a $500,000 deal  porting and developing new features
for a software application called comprehensive  apparel manufacturer’s package (CAMP).
Made by a firm called Data Basics,
CAMP was a kind of proto-ERP that US companies  used to manage textile imports from Asia.
The engagement was successful and led  to additional work with Data Basics.
## Patni to Infosys
The man leading the effort at  PCS was N. R. Narayana Murthy,
hired back in 1977 to be general manager  of PCS' growing software business.
A talented programmer and devout Hindu,  Murthy had once before started his own company
selling software in India but failed.  At PCS, he handled three jobs at once:
Data center management, computer sales  in India, and software export sales.
After four years of doing this and  visiting and understanding the US market,
he felt that he was ready to  try starting another company.
And believed that if he didn't do it  before turning 35, he would be cooked.
Six of his colleagues ended up joining him.
Funded with $250 from Murthy's wife, they  started Infosys in July 1981. The new business
quickly won over PCS's best customer Data  Basics, which sold the CAMP software.
But in those early days, Infosys did not have  enough money to buy their own computer to do
software development. So the company sent all  of its cofounders except Murthy to America
to work physically at the  client site. More body-shopping.
## Changing Times: A Focus on Software
India's IT sector grew within a socialist-minded,
nationalist framework that  emphasized self-reliance.
Nothing wrong with that, but there comes a  line when self-reliance tips into autarky.
By the mid-1980s, the Indian economy was  suffering from stifled growth and isolation.
Then came a series of major developments that  unlocked and supercharged the IT exports industry.
First, we had government reform.
In 1984, Rajiv Gandhi was elected as Prime  Minister after his mother's assassination.
Gandhi was technically savvy - a booster of  technology - and experienced first-hand the
issues of India's electronics policies whilst  organizing the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi.
His administration passed a series of new liberal  policies favoring software and hardware imports.
Tariffs on PCs imported for developing software  were cut from 135% to just 60%, and then zero a
few years later. Software tools for developing  other export software can be imported duty-free.
Many of these liberalizations were somewhat  walked back due to unstable economic and political
situations. Taxes on software and foreign travel  were hiked back up, for instance. But what stuck
helped software exports reach $96 million in 1990  - up from just $3.5 million ten years earlier.
Once upon a time, India's Department  of Electronics saw its role
as regulating electronics production and  protecting domestic manufacturing - i.e.
coddling India's biggest computer  manufacturer, ECIL. But in the 1980s,
that attitude shifted to promoting  software exports and private investment.
## Changing Times: Software Parks
Second were the Software  Technology Parks, or STPs.
The concept of an export processing  zone enjoying duty-free privileges
on imported equipment and relaxed labor  statutes isn't new even within India.
India was in fact one of the first Asian  countries to have them with the KASEZ in Gujarat.
A particularly special one was the Santacruz  Electronics EPZ in Mumbai. Created back in
1973 for electronics manufacturing, a few  software companies made their way there.
Citibank opened a software development  subsidiary inside. TCS and Tata Burroughs too.
The EDA firm Gateway Design Automation was there  too in be 1980s - they are perhaps most known
for producing the hardware  design language Verilog.
Some government officials started thinking about  a special zone to encourage software exports.
They would have the same duty-free and  labor privileges, but most importantly
the zones would have better  communication links with the US.
Few things more personified India's issues  than its massive communications problem.
The Indian telecommunications sector was  just not good. At the time it was perhaps
the world's most archaic, inadequate, overloaded  and inefficient phone system. The waiting list
for a landline telephone connection stretched half  a million long, and took 2-5 years of waiting.
Without more robust communications,
the Indian IT exports industry had no  choice but to rely on body-shopping.
Up into the late 1980s, 75-80% of India's  export earnings still came from body-shopping.
So it was a big deal when  Texas Instruments in 1985
installed a satellite data link between  the US and the Indian city of Bangalore.
They saw India as a good potential  market, a place for talent,
and they wanted to use the time zone differences  to achieve a 24-hour development cycle.
To get this satellite link installed, the  Indian Department of Electronics went to
bat for Texas Instruments. Hard. One DOE  veteran proudly said that they "broke 26
separate rules to accommodate TI's Bangalore  subsidiary and are willing to break more".
Like for instance, by law only the  Department of Telecommunications can
own and operate earth station equipment.  So the DOE worked out a paper agreement
where TI paid for the equipment but the  department ran and rented it out to TI.
Recognizing that campuses with shared resources  for compute, data communications links,
and other infrastructure can be a massive  boon for the software export industry,
the DOE began promoting the  Software Technology Parks in 1986.
However, the parks would not actually come  into being until 1991 - due to infighting
over the critical communications  links. But their data connections
helped the Indian IT giants leave behind  their old body-shopping practices.
Body shopping held a poor reputation.
It was also made less feasible by rule  changes in the early 1990s regarding
the US B-1 business visitor visa plus concerns  about the companies’ best talents hopping off.
Better communications enabled what Tata  Consultancy called the "offshore model".
A small team travels to the client site to collect  requirements and implement solutions. Meanwhile,
most of the development work is done in India,
where salaries are a third that  of what they are in the West.
It is true that Tata has been practicing  something like this since the earliest days
of their export service engagements. But then,
code had to be passed back and forth in  pouches by human couriers on flights.
Satellite comms links in the Software Parks  unlocked the offshore model’s full potential.
It also enabled new higher-value  services like business process
services outsourcing and call centers.  Onsite work - the long-disdained body
shopping - fell from 80+% in the late  1980s to just 59% by the late 1990s.
## Changing Times: Liberalizations
The STP policy arrived just before the more  famous 1991 liberalization - which had been
triggered by a significant  balance of payments crisis.
The liberalizations dismantled the  old License Raj, devalued the rupee,
and reduced barriers to foreign investment.  Foreign companies like Oracle, IBM, and HP
now had the opportunity to come to India to  setup their own software development shops.
The liberalizations also allowed  companies like Infosys to raise capital.
Infosys for their part went public in 1993  and used the money to build out their campus.
The flood of foreign hardware triggered by the  lowering of trade barriers also forced companies
like Wipro and Hindustan Computers Limited  to adopt the IT services export model.
Famously, Wipro was a vegetable oils manufacturer
that entered into minicomputers  and PCs after IBM's exit.
After 1991, they became an engineering  lab for hire - writing code for embedded
applications in telecom gear and computers
before moving to generalized software development  services for banks, retailers, and manufacturers.
Similar story for HCL. Founded by several  engineers who left behind another hardware maker,
HCL first made calculators and PCs. After  the import wave hit, they reorganized their
business around porting, driver development, and  onsite work. The hardware was later spun-off.
Together, Wipro and HCL or HCLTech - plus  a fifth named Tech Mahindra - round out
India's major IT services export giants.  Over 90% of their revenues come from abroad.
## I must always mention UNIX
The third (or fourth, I guess) factor I want  to bring up here might seem a bit strange,
but I think it is somewhat  underrated. India adopted UNIX.
UNIX is the famous operating system  created inside AT&T's Bell Labs.
It broke ground as a convenient programming  environment in which people can develop software,
but more importantly, its source code was widely  accessible in a sort of proto-open source way.
This was perfect for 1970s India. Imports  of finished software were restricted,
but source code imports were not.  Minicomputer makers like DCM and HCL
rapidly adopted UNIX - particularly  the Berkeley UNIX variant.
This allowed a generation of Indian programmers  to gain deep familiarity with UNIX - an effect
further enhanced by the Reserve Bank  of India famously recommending UNIX
as the standard OS for India's banks in 1985.
This familiarity became a boon when a  litany of UNIX variants like Sun's Solaris,
IBM's AIX, and HP's HP-UX became widely  embedded in the US corporate IT space.
Indian firms can develop on whatever  UNIX hardware they had, knowing
that it can work at a customer  site if they are also using UNIX.
## Y2K
The Y2K crisis was going to be the  end of the world. That time of urgency
with dogs eating cats, water flowing up into the  sky, and big pillars of light like in the movies.
Okay, maybe not. But fateful decisions by COBOL  developers to use two digits for a year to save
a little memory turned into what appeared  to be a looming disaster for computing.
Ah, so few things are more poetic  than a tiny, innocuous decision
coming around to bite us all in the butt.
Efforts to fix the "millennium bug" were  estimated to cost billions of dollars.
Were there even enough computer programmers in the  US to do it? The shortage seemed so severe that
the US government even raised its H-1 quota from  65,000 in 1998 to 115,000 in 1999 to handle it.
The Indian IT giants identified  Y2K as a massive opportunity.
They advertised in the US, emphasizing the  potential savings of using Indian labor.
Tata Consultancy set up a "Y2K office" in  Chennai dedicated solely to fixing Y2K code.
Each day, a thousand programmers churned out 2  million lines of COBOL code via a semi-automated,
17-step process, fixing Y2K bugs line by line.
All in all, Y2K made some $2.3 billion for the  Indian software industry in the late 1990s. TCS'
revenues soared from $125 million in 1995 to $419  million in 1999, whilst maintaining 32% margins.
Infosys earned over 20% of its 1998  and 1999 revenues just from Y2K.
In 1999, Infosys became the first Indian  company to issue ADRs on the US stock markets.
It allowed them to pay US employees in stock and  built up credibility with potential clients. And
it was just a good time to go public.
The IPO was a hit. The stock soared  nearly 50% from the offering price
and continued climbing soon after. By the end  of 1999, the stock had risen 10 times from
its IPO - giving the company a $20 billion market  cap and newfound prominence in the United States.
The other major IT outsourcer, TCS,  would be taken public a few years
later in 2004 - raising $1.2 billion in what  was then the largest IPO in Indian history.
## Post-Y2K
The impressive results from the Y2K drive  created many engineers trained in FORTRAN,
COBOL and other languages.
This convinced many customers to sign long  term agreements - generating repeat business
to maintain their software applications.  By 2001, over a quarter of the Fortune
1000 offshored their work - saving  up to 55% on their costs doing so.
Big companies like Hewlett-Packard,  Dell, Oracle, Microsoft, and Cisco
announced aggressive expansions  into India - investing billions
of dollars and creating tens of  thousands of new Indian jobs.
General Electric was a particularly notable  early adopter. After India liberalized in 1991,
GE made substantial early investments  - using Indian labor to help design
new fridges or jet engines at  half the cost of American labor.
Though they preferred to say  that they were getting 100%
more people onto a task. Potato, potahto.
In the 1990s, GE by itself contributed  50% of Wipro's software revenue
and 20-30% of Infosys' - a critical  booster in Indian credibility. In mid-2005,
the WSJ reported that GE still accounted for 15%  of Tata Consultancy Services' overseas revenue.
By 2001, India had 19 software parks. Fueled by  all this new money flooding into the country,
cities like Bangalore turned into boomtowns.
People started saying that India  had a Silicon Valley of its own.
## The Offshoring Debate
All this offshoring led to debates whether  India was stealing jobs from Americans.
Back in 2000, the companies explained their  offshoring as filling a talent gap - they said
it was "almost impossible" to find enough  good developers. Indian labor can fill the gap
by making software and services cheaper -  thus making American labor more productive.
But then the macroeconomy suffered a downturn in  2001 after the dotcom and telecom bubbles popped.
Companies then offshored their back offices -  maybe hiring an IT vendor like Wipro or TCS,
or opening their own India-based offices. It was  not so easy to argue talent shortage anymore.
By 2003, stories of job migration over  to India began hitting the mainstream.
Business Week broke the plane in February 2003  with a cover story titled "The New Global Job
Shift" - contrasting the boom in Bangalore  with that of decline in the United States.
That article asked: Can America lose these  critical knowledge work-based jobs like basic
research, chip design, and financial analysis and  still remain a global power? It cited an analyst
from Forrester Group saying that 3.3 million jobs  and $136 billion in wages will shift offshore.
The story got more attention throughout the year.  Tales of Americans training their replacements
before they lose their jobs went mainstream,  and it started to garner political attention.
For instance. In November 2003,  US Senator John Kerry - later 2004
US Presidential candidate and ketchup  scion (by marriage) - forwarded a bill
that would require call center workers to  identify where they physically were located.
Bad press canceled a 2003 Indiana  state government contract with Tata.
And the issue featured prominently  during the 2004 US presidential election,
with Kerry attacking incumbent President  Bush's stances on offshoring and pledging
to close "tax loopholes" that made it happen.  He called such companies "Benedict Arnolds".
There is no doubt that the stories hit hard  emotionally. Imagine how they might do on
TikTok today! Yet at the same time, the  data struggles to confirm on the aggregate
that offshoring actually leads to  layoffs, or that it is beneficial.
Numbers and methodologies  differ between researchers
too. Economists point out how impossible  it is to truly know whether those new
Indian workers actually replaced work  done or previously done by an American.
They also mention the recent post-bubble  recessions, rises in US worker productivity,
and also the fact that as India's  IT exports industry grows, they buy
more services from the US too. I shall  leave the debate to the comment section.
## Conclusion
In 2003, India delivered $9.5 billion of exports.
By 2013, that had grown to about $76  billion. And then in 2023, $194 billion.
Today, the sector as a whole is  directly responsible for 6 million jobs,
and 7-8% of India's GDP. With much of  that revenue still coming from abroad,
IT services exports offset  60% of India's trade deficit.
As late as 2023, the industry grew a fairly  strong 8.4%. But then in 2024 growth rapidly
decelerated to 3.8% - incremental revenue  falling from $19 billion to $9 billion.
Headcount growth slowed too. In 2023, the industry  as a whole added almost 300,000 jobs, per Nasscom.
A year later in 2024, it added only 60,000.
The biggest companies posted headcount declines.
In 2024, Infosys saw headcount reduced  by about 26,000 via attrition and reduced
hiring - the first such decline in the  company's record as a public entity.
Tata Consultancy's headcount declined by 13,000  in 2024 - the first decline since 2005. Then in
July 2025, they laid off 2% or 12,000 of their  employees - the company's largest layoff to date.
And of course, the stock. Since December 2024,  the share prices of both Infosys and TCS have
declined 40%. Their price multiples  compressing significantly as well.
This has been primarily attributed to AI. I  am struck by how similar the early jobs done
by Claude are to those ones done by the  IT exporters: Porting software, 24-hour
development cycles by submitting a long-running  job before going to bed, and other knowledge work.
The risk is that the LLMs eventually do  all the things that the IT exporters can.
Announcements from Anthropic of Claude plugins  for legal, finance and sales tasks in early 2026
not only sledgehammered the SaaS  stocks, but Infosys and TCS as well.
For what it is worth, the IT giants  have said that Generative AI will
eventually enhance rather than replace their work.
Enterprise customers still need integration,  governance, and trust. Productivity
going up will create savings that can be passed  to the client and additional margins to be kept.
But reaching that place will require  a crossover - and wading through that
fast-flowing river will be challenging. The  giants are now making their way through it,
and we shall see if they  all make it through intact.
